newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Imran Khan to fight on despite election failure.
newsitem.headline: Imran Khan to fight on despite election failure.

text.p: Former Pakistan cricket captain Imran Khan, who made no impact in national and provincial elections, said on Wednesday he expected to emerge as the main opposition and win the next polls.
"I think that next election, God willing, we will be unstoppable," he told Reuters Television in an interview.

"Whether it's the next election or the next one after that, there's no question of ever giving up until we bring about a change," he said after his newly-formed Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) failed to come even close to winning a seat in Monday's elections.

"We really didn't expect to do a lot better than we did," he said of a party formed last April and far from ready to contest the elections, which former prime minister Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League won in a landslide.
"It was really like pitting an under-19 cricket team against a professional test cricket team. But, really, we knew all that going in," he said.

Imran, 43, said he expected his party to take over as the national opposition from the Pakistan People's Party of Benazir Bhutto, sacked in November on disputed corruption charges and humiliated in the elections with just 18 seats in the 217-member National Assembly.
"We will, I think, be the only national opposition now because People's Party has been completely destroyed," he said.

Imran said the low turnout, officially around 40 percent, showed there was an opportunity for a third party appealing to those disenchanted by what he called a corrupt political mafia who saw elections as business and were prepared to spend huge amounts of money to win a seat.
"Then they have to get it back and they get it back through corruption. Hence the level of corruption increases every election," he said.
"I don't think the voting was more than 25 percent. That means 75 percent of the people did not vote. In that 75 percent, I feel, we are the ones who are going to tap it," Imran said.
"What they have shown is that they did not think we were ready. They did not think we were a viable force."
Imran said the elections had shortened the time needed to organise his party nationally.
"This is a great beginning. Now to strengthen this network will, I think, take about a year," he said.

Some analysts say Imran is unlikely ever to win power because of his playboy past and his marriage to 23-year-old Jemima Goldsmith, a convert to Islam and daughter of Anglo-French magnate Sir James Goldsmith, who is Jewish.
There have been widespread allegations of a "Zionist conspiracy" backing Imran that he said had been tough to fight.

"The Muslim League was very clever in the way they exploited this 'Jewish conspiracy'. They latched on to it and they really hammered it into the people in every speech how Israeli money has come in to support me," Imran said.
"You can use it in one election," he said. "Something that is so based on lies just cannot last. Sooner or later, people will see through this."
Imran said he would not change tactics despite Tehrik-i-Insaaf's election failure.

"Today, I could easily have, not perhaps won the election, but I could have been the second biggest party in Pakistan. All I had to do was to take professional politicians into my party, disgruntled politicians from both sides," he said.
"But that would not bring about a change in this country. Change can only come with new people who don't have a vested interest in protecting this system."
Nevertheless, Imran admitted he had difficulty drawing new people into election politics.

"It's not that there is a shortage of honest people. The problem is they're scared. They're scared because of the campaign I went through, the personal attacks, the mudslinging in the newspapers," he said.
"There's fear of political victimisation, which has happened time and time again."
